title: Cluster 01 DRILL: Viral Structure and the Phage Cycles
subtitle: H2 Biology 9477 · Book 4 · 8 questions · 76 marks · 31 parts · one mark per minute, so a little over an hour and a quarter · every question is an actual exam paper question
intro_html:
Answers sit directly under each part, hidden. Click Show answer only after you have said your full reasoning aloud for that part. Check (a) before you start (b), that is the point of the layout.

Rate your confidence before every reveal. A dashed line sits above each answer block. Say high, medium or guessed out loud before you click. A right answer said hesitantly stays ACTIVE; a right answer said confidently moves on.

Every question below is a real exam paper question. The stem is the paper's own wording, and the paper, year and question number are named in the Sources block at the foot of every question. Where a stem has been edited it is only so that it stands without the parts of the original that came before it, and the edit is written out in that same block. If a question cannot be traced to a paper, it is not in here.

Eight questions, 76 marks, 31 parts. The set is sized for coverage, not for the clock. Questions 1 to 4 are viral structure, the viral genome and the cell theory, 36 marks; questions 5 to 8 are the phage cycles, 40 marks. Two sittings is a reasonable way to run it.

The anchors. Question 4(a) is 9477 Specimen Paper 1 Question 3 word for word, the only official Cambridge item that exists on this cluster. Question 5(b) is SAJC's 2023 Paper 3 Section B essay at its real 10 marks, and it is the full-cycle question: the lytic cycle end to end, five stages, no shortcuts.

Six real figures, five questions figure-led. Book 4 runs at 43.8% figure-led overall and 45.7% among structured parts, higher than any Book so far, so nearly half of every structured question here opens with a diagram or a micrograph. Every figure is the real image from the paper the question came from, not a redrawing. Two further figures could not be recovered from their papers; those parts carry the paper's own description as prose instead, and say so.

No read-off-the-graph parts. The two graphs in this drill are stimulus for an explain question and nothing else. Question 6(b)'s graph carries no numbers at all, so the marks are for the induction mechanism, not for the trend.

Two MCQs, both real, both audited. The paper awards one mark for the letter. The drill then asks you to explain your answer, which is where every option has to be justified rather than three of them dismissed.

Cumulative over Books 1, 2 and 3. Q2(a) and Q2(c) need histones, linear chromosomes and chromosome number from Book 2. Q3(b), Q3(c) and Q3(d) need transcription, translation and DNA replication said cold. Q5(a) needs amino acids, peptide bonds and levels of protein structure from Book 1 held against nucleotides, phosphodiester bonds and the double helix from Book 2. A Book 1 or Book 2 gap surfacing here is worth more than a clean Cluster 1 answer, so say it out loud when it happens.

What the marks reward. Write capsid, not protein coat, on a labelling part. Write viral envelope, not phospholipid bilayer and not protein envelope. Keep the bilayer host-derived and the glycoproteins virally encoded, because a scheme prints a reject for saying both came from the previous host. Say template and synthesis, never conversion. Give every comparison point to point on the same feature. On any phage answer, the capsid is left outside the bacterial cell wall, and water enters by osmosis after lysozyme digests it.

One primary concept each, checked for duplicated required ANSWERS and not just for duplicated labels. Q1 reading an unfamiliar enveloped virus and saying where each part came from · Q2 three viruses that are on no syllabus, described on the axes the outcome names · Q3 what the genome type forces the virion to carry · Q4 the cell theory tested statement by statement · Q5 the lytic cycle end to end, plus protein against nucleic acid as molecules · Q6 why a phage would ever choose not to kill its host · Q7 phage anatomy mapped to function, and what happens when the receptor does not fit · Q8 the lytic cycle turned into a therapy, and where the therapy fails. The one shared idea in the set is that viruses are acellular, which Q4(b) needs alongside the crystallisation and ATP arguments and Q4(c) needs alongside the host-resources argument; the two parts are marked on different points and neither answer is the other. Every other pair was checked at the level of the paragraph the scheme demands, and no two questions need the same one.

Nothing from Books 5 to 9, and nothing from Clusters 2 or 3 of this Book. The influenza and HIV reproductive cycles, antigenic shift and drift, and the whole of bacterial genetics are later clusters, so no question here needs them. Where influenza appears it is only as a genome to compare against, at the level of eight negative-sense segments. Vaccines, antibodies and immunity are Extension Topic A and are out of scope in every answer.
